query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the grain boundary density in the FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating by refining its grain size will enhance its wear resistance and favor a deformation mechanism dominated by grain-boundary sliding rather than dislocation accumulation during high-temperature sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating with a baseline (coarser) grain structure produced via standard processing, on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled annealing or thermomechanical treatment to refine the grain size, thereby increasing the overall grain boundary density compared to the baseline condition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding contact conditions (e.g., operating at temperatures ≥700°C) where diffusion processes and microstructural stability are critical to wear and deformation behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary density – increased boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion and promote a shift to grain-boundary-mediated deformation.
generation.mechanism: The refined microstructure, characterized by a higher density of grain boundaries, limits the accumulation of dislocations and promotes more uniform, grain boundary sliding. This change reduces localized plastic deformation, leading to a lower wear rate under high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline, the grain-refined coating is expected to show reduced overall wear and a transition in microscopic deformation from dislocation pile-up to more distributed grain boundary sliding, with enhanced hardness and resistance to plastic flow.
generation.baseline: The conventional HEA coating with coarser grains, which exhibits higher wear due to localized dislocation accumulation and less effective accommodation of plastic deformation under high-temperature sliding.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under high-temperature sliding conditions where grain refinement remains stable; however, at temperatures high enough to induce excessive grain growth or phase transformations, the predicted benefits may not be realized.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement in wear resistance is uncertain and could be influenced by competing high-temperature effects such as elemental segregation or secondary phase formation at grain boundaries.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu HEA coatings on identical conventional metal substrates: one set with the baseline grain structure and one set that has undergone controlled grain refinement via annealing or thermomechanical treatment. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding wear tests (e.g., at temperatures ≥700°C) using a standardized tribometer.
measurements: Quantitative wear volume or mass loss measurements.
Microhardness testing to assess changes in mechanical properties.
Microscopic analysis (e.g., SEM/TEM) to evaluate the deformation mode (dislocation density versus grain boundary sliding).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the grain-refined coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and lack evidence of a shift to grain boundary-mediated deformation relative to the baseline, or if they show increased wear, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. From the viewpoint of applications in extrusion dies and cutting inserts, the cost of metal powders used to develop bulk HEAs can hinder their commercialization as an alternative to the alloys in use. However, coatings of high-performance HEAs on low-cost substrates can be considered as an economically viable way forward to counter the drawbacks of the coatings employed in harsh environments, such as commercial coatings for cutting tools, extrusion dies,

In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. frame.system: A FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy applied as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, initially in a baseline microstructural state suitable for high-temperature applications.
frame.goal: To establish a mechanistic understanding that links controlled microstructural modifications of the HEA coating to directional changes in overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding at high temperatures.
frame.limitation: The current uncertainty about which intrinsic (e.g., grain boundaries, phase stability, or elemental segregation) or extrinsic (e.g., substrate interaction, stress distribution) factors predominantly control wear behavior and deformation in the high-temperature sliding regime, and no single, verified mechanistic hypothesis exists that ties these aspects together with a falsifiable test.
root_cause_cues: controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition
specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis
constraints: The hypothesis must be single and testable.
A controlled change (e.g., variation in grain size, phase distribution, or secondary phase content) relative to a baseline condition must be defined.
Predictions must include directional changes in wear (e.g., reduction/increase) and microscopic deformation (e.g., harder/deformable microstructures).
The hypothesis must articulate the operating regime explicitly (high temperature sliding).
It must also include criteria for falsification.
frame.regime: High-temperature sliding contact conditions (e.g., temperatures at or above the service temperature of the coating where diffusion and microstructural stability are critical).
prior_attempts: Previous studies have linked grain size refinement and phase stability in HEA coatings to improvements in wear resistance, but lacked a controlled variable that isolates the mechanistic role during high-temperature sliding.

Other tribological experiments have observed correlations between elemental segregation at elevated temperatures and localized deformation mechanisms, yet they did not provide a single, integrated mechanistic hypothesis that predicts directional changes under controlled modifications.

decision.trend: Over the past few years, research on high-entropy alloy coatings has shifted from demonstrating that overall strength and oxidation resistance can be improved by introducing secondary phases or refining microstructure, to more targeted studies that correlate detailed microstructural characteristics with tribological behavior under high-temperature conditions. Early work established that processing routes (such as ball milling, sputtering, or laser cladding) can yield refined microstructures with enhanced hardness and strength. Later studies used controlled processing (for example, via annealing treatments) to modify grain size or precipitate distribution, and linked these changes to improvements in wear resistance and shifts in deformation mechanisms. However, none of the prior investigations have isolated a single microstructural variable—such as the grain boundary density—as the dominant contributor to wear and deformation during high-temperature sliding.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear whether the improved tribological behavior in high-temperature sliding is primarily governed by enhanced grain boundary mediated mechanisms (due to grain refinement) that inhibit dislocation accumulation, or by other factors such as phase stability or elemental segregation at the sliding interface. No study to date has provided a controlled experiment that directly ties a systematic change in grain size (and hence grain boundary density) to directional shifts in wear resistance and microscopic deformation under the high-temperature sliding contact regime.
decision.lever: systematically tuning the coating’s grain size (by a controlled annealing or thermomechanical treatment that refines grains relative to a baseline microstructure)
decision.why: This approach directly tests the hypothesis that increasing grain boundary density enhances wear resistance by limiting dislocation-driven plastic flow during high-temperature sliding. Prior evidence from coatings in similar systems (PMC7304825 and PMC10142552) shows that microstructural refinement improves hardness and adhesion, but the specific impact on sliding wear and the associated deformation mechanisms at elevated temperatures has not been isolated. A failure to observe the predicted reduction in wear or a shift toward more boundary-localized deformation when refining the grain structure would falsify the hypothesis.
